paper.title: UPPSC LT Grade Mathematics 2018 (29 July)
paper.source: UPPSC Assistant Teacher (LT grade) examination of 29 July 2018, Mathematics, booklet series C (DFMET-03): part II, questions 31 to 150, as shared after the exam; questions 119 to 126 are missing from the available copy
paper.note: The mathematics part; the whole paper had 150 questions in 2 hours. Questions 119 to 126 are missing from the available copy.

en.q: If $\theta$ is real, then
en.explanation: $\sin(i\theta)=\dfrac{e^{-\theta}-e^{\theta}}{2i}=\dfrac{i(e^{\theta}-e^{-\theta})}{2}=i\sinh\theta$. The others: $\cos(i\theta)=\cosh\theta$, $\tan(i\theta)=i\tanh\theta$, $\cot(i\theta)=-i\coth\theta$.

en.q: If $z=x+iy$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$, then $\left|\dfrac{z-3}{z+3}\right|=2$ represents a circle, whose centre and radius, respectively, are
notes: Sign of the centre and the radius are both wrong.
facts: $|z-a|=k|z-b|$ ($k\ne1$) is a circle (Apollonius); $k=1$ gives the perpendicular bisector.

en.q: If $\omega\,(\ne1)$ is a cube root of unity, then the value of $\{(1-\omega+\omega^2)^5+(1+\omega-\omega^2)^5-32\}$ is
en.explanation:
Since $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$: $1-\omega+\omega^2=-2\omega$ and $1+\omega-\omega^2=-2\omega^2$.
$(-2\omega)^5+(-2\omega^2)^5=-32(\omega^2+\omega)=32$.
So the value is $32-32=0$.
notes: Correct: the two powers add up to 32.
This is the sum of the two powers, before subtracting 32.
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem

en.q: The value of $\sqrt{3-4i}$ is
en.explanation: $(2-i)^2=4-4i+i^2=3-4i$. So $\sqrt{3-4i}=\pm(2-i)$, and $2-i$ is the option.
path: 10.5 Square root of a complex number
facts: Square each option: a quick test for $\sqrt{a+ib}$.

en.q: If $\cos(x+iy)=\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha$, then the value of $(\cosh 2y+\cos 2x)$ is
en.explanation:
$\cos(x+iy)=\cos x\cosh y-i\sin x\sinh y$, so $\cos x\cosh y=\cos\alpha$ and $\sin x\sinh y=-\sin\alpha$.
Squaring and adding: $\cos^2x\cosh^2y+\sin^2x\sinh^2y=1$, which simplifies to $\cos^2x+\sinh^2y=1$.
$\cosh2y+\cos2x=(1+2\sinh^2y)+(2\cos^2x-1)=2(\sinh^2y+\cos^2x)=2$.
notes: This is $\cos^2x+\sinh^2y$, not the required sum.
Impossible: $\cosh2y\ge1$ and $\cos2x\ge-1$, so the sum is never negative.
path: 10.8 Separation into real and imaginary parts

en.q: The three cube roots of $z=-8i$ are
en.explanation:
$-8i=8e^{-i\pi/2}$, so the roots are $2e^{i(-\pi/6+2k\pi/3)}$, $k=0,1,2$.
Angles $-30^\circ, 90^\circ, 210^\circ$ give $\sqrt3-i,\ 2i,\ -\sqrt3-i$.
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem
facts: The $n$ cube roots lie on a circle, $120^\circ$ apart; they add up to 0.

en.q: If $\mathrm{Im}\left(\dfrac{z-1}{2z+1}\right)=-4$, then the locus of $z$ is
en.explanation:
With $z=x+iy$: $\dfrac{(x-1)+iy}{(2x+1)+2iy}$ has imaginary part $\dfrac{y(2x+1)-2y(x-1)}{(2x+1)^2+4y^2}=\dfrac{3y}{(2x+1)^2+4y^2}$.
So $3y=-4[(2x+1)^2+4y^2]$, i.e. $16x^2+16y^2+16x+3y+4=0$: equal $x^2,y^2$ coefficients and no $xy$ term, a circle.
notes: $x^2$ and $y^2$ have equal coefficients, so not an ellipse proper.
Only if the second-degree terms vanished.
facts: $x^2+y^2$ with equal coefficients and no $xy$ term means a circle.

en.q: If $f(z)=(x^2+ay^2)+ibxy$ is a complex analytic function of $z=x+iy$, then the value of $a+b$ is
en.explanation:
$u=x^2+ay^2$, $v=bxy$.
$u_x=v_y$: $2x=bx\Rightarrow b=2$. $u_y=-v_x$: $2ay=-by\Rightarrow a=-1$.
So $a+b=1$.
notes: That is $a$ alone; a sign slip in $u_y=-v_x$ would give $a=1$, $a+b=3$.

en.q: Which one of the following is false?
en.explanation:
For $|z|^2=x^2+y^2$: $u_x=2x$, $v_y=0$, $u_y=2y$, $v_x=0$; C–R hold only at $z=0$.
So $|z|^2$ is differentiable only at the single point 0 and analytic nowhere (analyticity needs a neighbourhood). Statement (c) is false.
notes: True: C–R fail everywhere for $\bar z$.
False: differentiable at 0 only, not analytic.
facts: Analytic at a point means differentiable in a whole neighbourhood of it.

en.q: For $z\in\mathbb C$, the inequality $|z+i|>|z-i|$ is
en.explanation:
$|z+i|^2-|z-i|^2=(x^2+(y+1)^2)-(x^2+(y-1)^2)=4y$.
So the inequality holds exactly when $y=\mathrm{Im}\,z>0$: $z$ is nearer to $i$ than to $-i$.
notes: The real part does not enter: the difference is $4y$.
facts: $|z-a|>|z-b|$ is the half-plane on $b$'s side of the perpendicular bisector of $ab$.

en.q: The value of $\int_{-3}^{3}\frac{x^2}{1+3^x}\,dx$ is
en.explanation:
Replace $x$ by $-x$: $\dfrac{x^2}{1+3^{-x}}=\dfrac{3^x x^2}{1+3^x}$. Adding the two forms, $2I=\int_{-3}^{3}x^2\,dx=18$.
So $I=9$.

en.q: The area bounded by the curves $y=\sin x$, $y=\cos x$ and $y$-axis is
en.explanation:
The curves meet first at $x=\pi/4$; between $0$ and $\pi/4$, $\cos x\ge\sin x$.
$$\int_0^{\pi/4}(\cos x-\sin x)\,dx=[\sin x+\cos x]_0^{\pi/4}=\sqrt2-1$$
notes: Sign slip at the lower limit.
facts: $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ cross at $\pi/4$, where both equal $1/\sqrt2$.

en.q: If $\lim_{x\to2}\frac{\sqrt{ax+b}-3}{x-2}=\frac12$, then the value of $a,\ b$ will be
en.explanation:
For a finite limit the numerator must vanish at 2: $\sqrt{2a+b}=3$, so $2a+b=9$.
Then the limit is the derivative $\dfrac{a}{2\sqrt{2a+b}}=\dfrac a6=\dfrac12$, so $a=3$, $b=3$.
facts: A finite limit of a $\frac{?}{0}$ form forces the numerator to vanish too.

en.q: Consider the following statements: I. $y=|x|$ is differentiable at $x=0$. II. $y=x|x|$ is differentiable everywhere. Which of the above statements is/are true?
en.explanation:
I: the one-sided derivatives of $|x|$ at 0 are $-1$ and $1$; not differentiable. False.
II: $x|x|$ is $x^2$ for $x\ge0$ and $-x^2$ for $x<0$; its derivative $2|x|$ exists everywhere. True.

en.q: If $\dfrac1u=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$, then $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}+y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}+z\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z}$ is equal to
en.explanation:
$u=(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{-1/2}$ is homogeneous of degree $-1$.
By Euler's theorem the sum equals $(-1)u=-u$.
facts: Euler: $\sum x\,u_x=nu$ for $u$ homogeneous of degree $n$.

en.q: The differential equation of the straight lines at a fixed distance $p$ from the origin is
en.explanation:
Such lines are $y=mx+c$ with $\dfrac{|c|}{\sqrt{1+m^2}}=p$.
Eliminate: $m=y'$, $c=y-xy'$, so $(y-xy')^2=p^2(1+y'^2)$, i.e. $(xy'-y)^2=p^2(1+y'^2)$.

en.q: The solution of the differential equation $y-x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=a\left(y^2+\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)$ is
en.explanation:
Rearrange: $y-ay^2=(x+a)\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, so $\dfrac{dy}{y(1-ay)}=\dfrac{dx}{x+a}$.
$\int\left(\dfrac1y+\dfrac{a}{1-ay}\right)dy=\ln\dfrac{y}{1-ay}=\ln(x+a)+\text{const}$.
So $y=k(x+a)(1-ay)$, i.e. $(x+a)(1-ay)=cy$.

en.q: The value of $c$ in Lagrange's mean value theorem for $f(x)=x(x-1)$ in $[1,2]$ is
en.explanation:
$\dfrac{f(2)-f(1)}{2-1}=\dfrac{2-0}{1}=2$ and $f'(c)=2c-1$.
$2c-1=2\Rightarrow c=\dfrac32$.
notes: Correct; for a quadratic $c$ is always the midpoint.
facts: For a quadratic, the Lagrange point $c$ is the midpoint of the interval.

en.q: If $x=a(\cos t+t\sin t)$, $y=a(\sin t-t\cos t)$, then the value of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is
en.explanation:
$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=at\cos t$, $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=at\sin t$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\tan t$.
$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\sec^2t}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{\sec^2t}{at\cos t}=\dfrac{\sec^3t}{at}$.

en.q: If $\lim_{x\to0}x\sin\frac1x=A$ and $\lim_{x\to\infty}x\sin\frac1x=B$, then which of the following is true?
en.explanation:
$|x\sin(1/x)|\le|x|\to0$, so $A=0$.
With $t=1/x\to0$: $x\sin(1/x)=\dfrac{\sin t}{t}\to1$, so $B=1$.
facts: Bounded times a quantity tending to 0 tends to 0 (sandwich).

en.q: The solution of the differential equation $(x+2y^3)\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y$, $y(0)=1$ is
en.explanation:
Treat $x$ as a function of $y$: $\dfrac{dx}{dy}-\dfrac{x}{y}=2y^2$, linear with integrating factor $\dfrac1y$.
$\dfrac{d}{dy}\left(\dfrac xy\right)=2y\Rightarrow \dfrac xy=y^2+C$. At $y=1$, $x=0$: $C=-1$.
So $x=y^3-y$, i.e. $x+y-y^3=0$.
notes: Sign of $x$ reversed: $x=y-y^3$ does not satisfy the equation.
Passes through $(0,1)$, but $x=2y-2y^3$ does not satisfy the equation.
facts: If $dy/dx$ has $y^n$ terms with $x$ linear, solve for $x$ as a function of $y$.

en.q: $\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac{e^{1/x}-1}{e^{1/x}+1}$ is equal to
The function $\phi(x)=(x-a)^m(x-b)^n$ satisfies the conditions of Rolle's theorem, when
en.explanation:
For positive integers $m,n$, $\phi$ is a polynomial: continuous and differentiable everywhere, and $\phi(a)=\phi(b)=0$.
Rolle's theorem is stated on $[a,b]$, which needs $a<b$. Both conditions together: option (b). Option (a) leaves out $a<b$: for $a=b$ there is no interval at all, and for $a>b$ the theorem has to be applied on $[b,a]$ instead.
notes: Enough for the function, but the interval $[a,b]$ also needs $a<b$.
Correct: polynomial, equal end values on $[a,b]$.
With $a<b$ alone, $m,n$ could be negative or fractional, and $\phi$ may then be undefined or unbounded on $[a,b]$.

en.q: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a differentiable function such that $f'(x^2)=4x^2-1$ for $x>0$ and $f(1)=1$. Then $f(4)$ is
If $y=x^{x^{x^{\cdots\text{to infinity}}}}$, then $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is equal to
en.explanation:
$y=x^y$, so $\ln y=y\ln x$.
Differentiate: $\dfrac{y'}{y}=y'\ln x+\dfrac yx$, so $y'\left(\dfrac1y-\ln x\right)=\dfrac yx$.
Hence $x\,y'=\dfrac{y^2}{1-y\ln x}$.

en.q: If $x=t$, $y=\log_e(\cos t)$, $t\in\left[0,\dfrac\pi4\right]$, then the value of $\int_0^{\pi/4}\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt$ is
en.explanation:
$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=1$, $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\tan t$, so the integrand is $\sqrt{1+\tan^2t}=\sec t$.
$\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec t\,dt=[\ln(\sec t+\tan t)]_0^{\pi/4}=\ln(\sqrt2+1)$.

en.q: The value of $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{n+2}+\cdots+\frac1{6n}\right]$ is
en.explanation: The sum is $\sum_{r=1}^{5n}\frac1n\cdot\frac{1}{1+r/n}\to\int_0^5\frac{dx}{1+x}=\ln6$.
notes: There are $5n$ terms, each about $1/n$; the sum does not vanish.
This is the limit up to $\frac1{2n}$.
This is the limit up to $\frac1{3n}$.

en.q: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\sin\frac an\right)^n$ is equal to
en.explanation:
A $1^\infty$ form: the limit is $e^{L}$ with $L=\lim n\sin\dfrac an=\lim a\cdot\dfrac{\sin(a/n)}{a/n}=a$.
So the limit is $e^a$.

en.q: The value of $\int_0^{1000}e^{x-[x]}\,dx$ is
en.explanation: $x-[x]$ has period 1, so the integral is $1000\int_0^1e^x\,dx=1000(e-1)$.

en.q: The value of $\int x^2e^x\,dx$ is
en.explanation: By parts twice: $\int x^2e^x\,dx=x^2e^x-2\int xe^x\,dx=x^2e^x-2(x-1)e^x=(x^2-2x+2)e^x+c$.
notes: Sign of the middle term: differentiate to check.

en.q: The value of $\int_0^\infty\frac{x\,dx}{(1+x)(1+x^2)}$ is
en.explanation:
$\dfrac{x}{(1+x)(1+x^2)}=-\dfrac{1}{2(1+x)}+\dfrac{x+1}{2(1+x^2)}$.
Antiderivative: $\dfrac14\ln\dfrac{1+x^2}{(1+x)^2}+\dfrac12\tan^{-1}x$. The log term is 0 at both ends, so the value is $\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac\pi2=\dfrac\pi4$.
facts: Over $(0,\infty)$, $x\mapsto1/x$ shows $\int\frac{x\,dx}{(1+x)(1+x^2)}=\int\frac{dx}{(1+x)(1+x^2)}$, and they add to $\pi/2$.

en.q: If $u=(x^2+y^2)^{\frac12}$ and $x^3+y^3+3axy=5a^3$, then the value of $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ at $(a,a)$ is
en.explanation:
From the curve: $3x^2+3y^2y'+3ay+3axy'=0$, so $y'=-\dfrac{x^2+ay}{y^2+ax}=-1$ at $(a,a)$.
$\dfrac{du}{dx}=\dfrac{x+yy'}{u}=\dfrac{a-a}{a\sqrt2}=0$, which is not among (a)–(c).
The booklet prints $5a^2$; the point $(a,a)$ lies on the curve only with $5a^3$. The slope $y'$ at $(a,a)$ does not involve the constant, so the answer is 0 either way.

en.q: A solution of the differential equation $\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dy+\sqrt{1-y^2}\,dx=0$ $(|x|<1,\ |y|<1)$ is
en.explanation:
Separate: $\dfrac{dy}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}+\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=0$, so $\sin^{-1}x+\sin^{-1}y=k$.
Taking sine: $\sin(\sin^{-1}x+\sin^{-1}y)=x\sqrt{1-y^2}+y\sqrt{1-x^2}=c$.

en.q: If $u=\log\dfrac{x^3+y^3}{x+y}$, then the value of $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}+y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}$ is
en.explanation:
$e^u=\dfrac{x^3+y^3}{x+y}$ is homogeneous of degree 2.
For $u=\log f$ with $f$ of degree $n$: $xu_x+yu_y=n=2$.

en.q: If $x+2y=8$, then the maximum value of $xy$ is
en.explanation:
$xy=(8-2y)y=8y-2y^2$, maximum at $y=2$: $16-8=8$ (with $x=4$).
Or AM–GM: $x\cdot2y\le\left(\frac{x+2y}{2}\right)^2=16$, so $xy\le8$.
notes: This is the maximum of $x\cdot2y$, not $xy$.

en.q: The equation of the tangent at $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$ to the curve $x=a(\theta+\sin\theta)$, $y=a(1+\cos\theta)$ is
en.explanation:
$\dfrac{dx}{d\theta}=a(1+\cos\theta)=a$, $\dfrac{dy}{d\theta}=-a\sin\theta=-a$, so the slope is $-1$.
Point: $\left(a(\frac\pi2+1),\ a\right)$. Tangent: $y-a=-\left(x-a(\frac\pi2+1)\right)$, i.e. $x+y=a\left(\frac\pi2+2\right)$.
notes: Forgets the $+a$ terms of the point.

en.q: The area bounded by the curves $y=|x|-1$ and $y=-|x|+1$ is
en.explanation:
The two curves form a square with vertices $(\pm1,0)$ and $(0,\pm1)$.
Its diagonals are 2 and 2, so the area is $\frac12\cdot2\cdot2=2$.
notes: Twice the side $\sqrt2$; the area is side$^2=2$.

en.q: The slope of the tangent at the point $P(x,y)$ on a curve is $-\dfrac{y+3}{x+2}$. If the curve passes through the origin, then the equation of the curve is
en.explanation:
$\dfrac{dy}{y+3}=-\dfrac{dx}{x+2}$ gives $(x+2)(y+3)=C$. Through $(0,0)$: $C=6$.
So $xy+3x+2y+6=6$, i.e. $xy+2y+3x=0$.

en.q: If $y(x)$ is a solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2xy=x$, $y(0)=0$ then $\lim_{x\to\infty}y(x)$ is
en.explanation:
Integrating factor $e^{x^2}$: $ye^{x^2}=\int xe^{x^2}dx=\frac12e^{x^2}+C$. $y(0)=0$ gives $C=-\frac12$.
So $y=\frac12-\frac12e^{-x^2}\to\frac12$.
notes: The limit is $+\frac12$: the $C$ term carries $e^{-x^2}\to0$.

en.q: If $y=y(x)$ and $\dfrac{2+\sin x}{y+1}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)=-\cos x$, $y(0)=1$, then $y\left(\dfrac\pi2\right)$ is equal to
en.explanation:
$\dfrac{dy}{y+1}=-\dfrac{\cos x\,dx}{2+\sin x}$, so $\ln(y+1)=-\ln(2+\sin x)+k$, i.e. $(y+1)(2+\sin x)=C$.
$y(0)=1$: $C=4$. At $\frac\pi2$: $(y+1)\cdot3=4$, so $y=\frac13$.

en.q: The mean weight of 9 items is 15 kg. If one more item is added, the mean weight becomes 16 kg. Then the weight of the 10th item is
en.explanation:
Total of 9 items $=9\times15=135$ kg; total of 10 items $=10\times16=160$ kg.
The 10th item weighs $160-135=25$ kg.
facts: New item $=$ new total $-$ old total; shortcut: $16+9\times(16-15)=25$.

en.q: A coin is thrown 6 times. The probability of getting exactly four heads is
en.explanation: Binomial with $n=6$, $p=\frac12$: $P(X=4)=\binom64\left(\frac12\right)^6=\dfrac{15}{64}$.
path: 16.5 Bernoulli trials and the binomial distribution

en.q: A bag contains 8 red and 5 white balls. Three balls are drawn at random. The probability that one ball is red and two balls are white, is
en.explanation:
Favourable: $\binom81\binom52=8\times10=80$. Total: $\binom{13}{3}=286$.
Probability $=\dfrac{80}{286}=\dfrac{40}{143}$.
path: 16.1 Basic probability and the addition theorem

en.q: The mean of 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 4 is $n$. The numbers 3, 2, 2, 4, 3, $p$, 3 have mean $n-1$ and median $q$. Then $p+q$ is
en.explanation:
$n=\frac{24}{6}=4$. Second set: $\frac{17+p}{7}=3$, so $p=4$.
Ordered: 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4; the median (4th value) is $q=3$. So $p+q=7$.
facts: For an odd number $N$ of values, the median is the $\frac{N+1}{2}$th value in order.

en.q: If a hyperbola, whose parametric equations are $x=ct$, $y=\dfrac ct$, meets any circle with centre at $(0,0)$ in four points, determined by the parametric values $t_1,t_2,t_3$ and $t_4$, then the value of $t_1t_2t_3t_4$ is
en.explanation:
Put the point in $x^2+y^2=r^2$: $c^2t^2+\dfrac{c^2}{t^2}=r^2$, i.e. $c^2t^4-r^2t^2+c^2=0$.
The product of the four roots is $\dfrac{c^2}{c^2}=1$.
facts: For $xy=c^2$ and a circle centred at the origin, $t_1t_2t_3t_4=1$.

en.q: The product of the perpendiculars drawn from the foci of an ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ on any tangent to it, is
en.explanation:
Tangent $y=mx+\sqrt{a^2m^2+b^2}$, foci $(\pm ae,0)$.
Product $=\dfrac{(a^2m^2+b^2)-a^2e^2m^2}{1+m^2}=\dfrac{b^2m^2+b^2}{1+m^2}=b^2$ (using $a^2-a^2e^2=b^2$).
notes: That is the product when the major axis is along the $y$-axis ($b>a$).
facts: Product of focal perpendiculars on any tangent of an ellipse $=b^2$.

en.q: Let $y=mx+c$ be the equation of normal to the parabola $y^2=4ax$ at $(am^2,-2am)$. Then $c$ is equal to
en.explanation:
The point is $(at^2,2at)$ with $t=-m$. The normal there is $y=-tx+2at+at^3$.
With $t=-m$: $y=mx-2am-am^3$, so $c=-2am-am^3$.
notes: Sign error: correct for the point $(am^2,2am)$ with slope $-m$.
facts: Normal of $y^2=4ax$ in slope form: $y=mx-2am-am^3$, foot $(am^2,-2am)$.

en.q: If the sum of the slopes of the lines $x^2-2\lambda xy-7y^2=0$ is four times their product, then the value of $\lambda$ is
en.explanation:
With $y=mx$: $7m^2+2\lambda m-1=0$. Sum of slopes $=-\dfrac{2\lambda}{7}$, product $=-\dfrac17$.
$-\dfrac{2\lambda}{7}=-\dfrac47\Rightarrow\lambda=2$.
notes: Sign slip in the sum of slopes.

en.q: The distance between the foci of a hyperbola is 16 units and its eccentricity is $\sqrt2$. Its equation is
facts: $e=\sqrt2$ exactly when the hyperbola is rectangular ($a=b$).

en.q: For what values of $k$, the line $y=kx+2$ will be tangent to the conic $4x^2-9y^2=36$?
en.explanation:
The conic is $\dfrac{x^2}{9}-\dfrac{y^2}{4}=1$. Tangency of $y=mx+c$: $c^2=a^2m^2-b^2$.
$4=9k^2-4\Rightarrow k^2=\dfrac89\Rightarrow k=\pm\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}$.

en.q: The locus of the centres of circles, that passes through the origin and cuts off a length 6 from the line $y=4$, is
en.explanation:
Centre $(h,k)$, radius$^2=h^2+k^2$ (through the origin). Distance to $y=4$ is $|k-4|$; half-chord 3.
$h^2+k^2=9+(k-4)^2\Rightarrow h^2+8k-25=0$. Locus: $x^2+8y-25=0$.
facts: Chord length $=2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}$, $d$ the distance of the centre from the line.

en.q: The image of the point $(3,5,7)$ in the plane $2x+y+z=6$ is
The direction cosines of a line segment whose projections on the coordinate axes are $-6,3,2$, are
en.explanation: Length $=\sqrt{36+9+4}=7$. Projection on an axis $=$ length $\times$ cosine, so the direction cosines are $-\frac67,\frac37,\frac27$.
notes: The sign of the $x$-projection is lost.
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line
facts: Projections on the axes are $l\cdot L,\ m\cdot L,\ n\cdot L$ for a segment of length $L$.

en.q: If the lines $\dfrac{x-2}{3}=\dfrac{y-3}{4}=\dfrac{z-4}{5}$ and $\dfrac{x-1}{a}=\dfrac{y-2}{3}=\dfrac{z-3}{4}$ are coplanar, then $a$ is equal to
facts: Two lines are coplanar iff $[\vec a_2-\vec a_1,\ \vec b_1,\ \vec b_2]=0$.

en.q: The length of perpendicular from $(1,2,3)$ to the line $\dfrac{x-6}{3}=\dfrac{y-7}{2}=\dfrac{z-7}{-2}$ is
notes: This is the projection of $\vec{PA}$ on the line, not the distance.
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line
facts: Distance from a point to a line $=\sqrt{|\vec{PA}|^2-(\text{projection on the line})^2}$.

en.q: If $\cos\alpha,\cos\beta,\cos\gamma$ are the direction cosines of a straight line, then $(\sin^2\alpha+\sin^2\beta+\sin^2\gamma)$ is equal to
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line

en.q: The radius of the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2-x-y-z=0$ is
en.explanation: Centre $\left(\frac12,\frac12,\frac12\right)$, $d=0$. Radius $=\sqrt{\frac14+\frac14+\frac14}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

en.q: The conic $5x^2-6xy+5y^2+26x-22y+29=0$ represents
en.explanation:
$a=5,\ h=-3,\ b=5$: $h^2-ab=9-25<0$, so an ellipse type; $\Delta=-128\ne0$.
Centre $(-2,1)$; shifting gives $5X^2-6XY+5Y^2=8$, a real ellipse: rotating $45^\circ$ gives $2X'^2+8Y'^2=8$, i.e. $\frac{X'^2}{4}+Y'^2=1$ (semi-axes 2 and 1).

en.q: If $A$ is a $3\times3$ non-singular matrix, then $\det(\mathrm{adj}\,A)$ is equal to
en.explanation: $A\,\mathrm{adj}A=|A|I_3$ gives $|A|\,|\mathrm{adj}A|=|A|^3$, so $|\mathrm{adj}A|=|A|^2$.

en.q: The composite mapping $f\circ g$ of the maps $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=\sin x$ and $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $g(x)=x^2$ is
en.explanation: $(f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))=f(x^2)=\sin(x^2)$.

en.q: A square matrix $P$ satisfies $P^2=I-P$. If $P^n=5I-8P$, then $n$ is equal to
facts: If $P^2=I-P$, the coefficients of $P^n$ follow the Fibonacci numbers with alternating signs.

en.q: The number of solutions of $\log_4(x-1)=\log_2(x-3)$ is
en.explanation:
$\log_4(x-1)=\frac12\log_2(x-1)$, so $x-1=(x-3)^2$ with $x>3$.
$x^2-7x+10=0\Rightarrow x=2$ or $5$; only $x=5$ satisfies $x>3$. One solution.
facts: $\log_{a^k}x=\frac1k\log_ax$; always check the domain after squaring.

en.q: The eigenvalues of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}a&h&g\\0&b&0\\0&c&c\end{bmatrix}$ are
en.explanation:
Expand $|A-\lambda I|$ along the first column: $(a-\lambda)\begin{vmatrix}b-\lambda&0\\c&c-\lambda\end{vmatrix}=(a-\lambda)(b-\lambda)(c-\lambda)$.
Eigenvalues $a,b,c$.
facts: Eigenvalues of a triangular (or block-triangular) matrix are its diagonal entries.

en.q: A cyclic group having only one generator can have at most
en.explanation:
If $g$ generates $G$, so does $g^{-1}$. A unique generator forces $g=g^{-1}$, i.e. $g^2=e$.
So $|G|\le2$ (equivalently $\phi(n)=1$ only for $n=1,2$).
notes: The trivial group qualifies, but so does $\mathbb Z_2$.
facts: A cyclic group of order $n$ has $\phi(n)$ generators.

en.q: Every diagonal element of a skew-symmetric matrix is
en.explanation: $a_{ii}=-a_{ii}$ gives $a_{ii}=0$.
notes: That is for skew-Hermitian matrices (zero or purely imaginary).
facts: Skew-symmetric: zero diagonal; skew-Hermitian: diagonal zero or purely imaginary.

en.q: The number of real solutions of the equation $|x|^2+5|x|+4=0$ is
en.explanation:
With $t=|x|\ge0$: $t^2+5t+4=(t+1)(t+4)=0$ gives $t=-1,-4$, both negative.
No real solution.
notes: Correct: the left side is at least 4.

en.q: The sum of the infinite series $1-\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac12+\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac1{2^2}-\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac56\cdot\dfrac1{2^3}+\cdots\infty$ is
en.explanation:

With $x=\frac12$: sum $=\left(\frac32\right)^{-1/2}=\sqrt{\dfrac23}$.

en.explanation:
$G^2=AH=4A$. Then $2A+4A=27$, so $A=\frac92$ and $G^2=18$.
Sum 9, product 18: the numbers are 3 and 6.

en.q: Let $G$ be a group with identity element $e$. Let $a,b\in G$ be such that $a^5=e$ and $aba^{-1}=b^2$. Then $o(b)$ is
en.explanation:
Conjugating repeatedly: $a^kba^{-k}=b^{2^k}$. With $k=5$: $b=a^5ba^{-5}=b^{32}$, so $b^{31}=e$.
31 is prime, so $o(b)=31$ (for $b\ne e$).

en.q: Every square matrix can be expressed as
options: sum of symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
en.explanation: $A=\frac12(A+A')+\frac12(A-A')$: the first part is symmetric, the second skew-symmetric.
notes: Correct, and the split is unique.

en.q: The sum of the infinite series $\dfrac{1}{2!}+\dfrac{1+2}{3!}+\dfrac{1+2+3}{4!}+\dfrac{1+2+3+4}{5!}+\cdots\infty$ is
en.explanation:
$n$th term $=\dfrac{n(n+1)/2}{(n+1)!}=\dfrac{1}{2\,(n-1)!}$.
Sum $=\frac12\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{(n-1)!}=\dfrac e2$.

en.q: The characteristic roots of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}5&4\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ are
en.explanation: $\lambda^2-(\text{trace})\lambda+\det=\lambda^2-7\lambda+6=0$, so $\lambda=1,6$.
facts: For a $2\times2$ matrix: sum of eigenvalues = trace, product = determinant.

en.q: For square matrices $A$ and $B$, which of the following is true?
en.explanation:
Transpose is linear: $(A+B)'=A'+B'$.
The product rules reverse the order: $(AB)'=B'A'$, $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$; and inverse is not additive.

en.q: The characteristic roots of a Hermitian matrix are
en.explanation: If $Ax=\lambda x$ with $A^\theta=A$, then $\lambda\,x^\theta x=x^\theta Ax=\overline{\lambda}\,x^\theta x$, so $\lambda=\bar\lambda$: real.
notes: That is for skew-Hermitian matrices (or zero).
facts: Hermitian: real eigenvalues; skew-Hermitian: purely imaginary or zero; unitary: modulus 1.

en.q: The generator/generators of the cyclic group $\{a,a^2,a^3,a^4=e\}$ is/are
en.explanation:
In a cyclic group of order 4, $a^k$ generates iff $\gcd(k,4)=1$: $k=1,3$.
So the generators are $a$ and $a^3$.
facts: $a^k$ generates a cyclic group of order $n$ iff $\gcd(k,n)=1$.

en.q: The value of the determinant $\begin{vmatrix}43&1&6\\35&7&4\\17&3&2\end{vmatrix}$ is
en.explanation:
$C_1=C_2+7C_3$: $43=1+42$, $35=7+28$, $17=3+14$.
So $C_1-C_2-7C_3$ is a zero column and the determinant is 0.
facts: A determinant is 0 if one column is a combination of the others.

en.explanation:

Inverse of $-2$: $-2+b+1=-1\Rightarrow b=0$.
notes: Treats $*$ as ordinary addition (identity 0); here the identity is $-1$.

en.explanation:

en.q: Let $*$ be a binary operation defined on the set of positive rational numbers $\mathbb Q^+$ by the rule $a*b=\dfrac{ab}{3}$, $\forall a,b\in\mathbb Q^+$. Then the inverse of $4*6$ is
en.explanation:
Identity: $\frac{ae}{3}=a\Rightarrow e=3$. $4*6=\frac{24}{3}=8$.
Inverse of 8: $\frac{8b}{3}=3\Rightarrow b=\frac98$.
facts: For $a*b=\frac{ab}{k}$ on $\mathbb Q^+$: identity $k$, inverse of $a$ is $\frac{k^2}{a}$.

$f$ is an odd function and $g$ is an even function

notes: $\sin x$ is odd, but $\sin|x|$ is even.

en.q: If $f(x)=\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x^2\\x&x^2&1\\x^2&1&x\end{vmatrix}$, then the value of $f(\sqrt[3]{3})$ is
Let $R$ be a relation on a set $A$ and let $I_A$ denote the identity relation on $A$. Then $R$ is antisymmetric, if and only if
en.explanation:
Antisymmetric: $(a,b)\in R$ and $(b,a)\in R$ imply $a=b$.
$(a,b)\in R\cap R^{-1}$ means exactly both pairs are in $R$, so the condition says $R\cap R^{-1}\subseteq I_A$.
facts: Symmetric: $R=R^{-1}$; antisymmetric: $R\cap R^{-1}\subseteq I_A$; transitive: $R\circ R\subseteq R$.

en.q: If $x$ is the first term of a geometric progression and the sum of its infinite terms is $\dfrac13$, then $x$ lies in the interval
en.explanation: $\dfrac{x}{1-r}=\dfrac13\Rightarrow r=1-3x$. Convergence needs $-1<1-3x<1$, i.e. $0<x<\dfrac23$.

en.q: If $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^n=s$, $|r|<1$, then $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^{2n}$ is equal to
en.explanation: $s=\frac1{1-r}$, so $r=\frac{s-1}{s}$. Then $\sum r^{2n}=\dfrac1{1-r^2}=\dfrac{s^2}{s^2-(s-1)^2}=\dfrac{s^2}{2s-1}$.
notes: That is $\sum r^n$ squared, a different series.

en.q: The infinite series $\dfrac1{1^p}+\dfrac1{2^p}+\dfrac1{3^p}+\dfrac1{4^p}+\cdots\infty$ is convergent, if
en.explanation: The $p$-series converges iff $p>1$ (integral test: $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx$ is finite iff $p>1$).

en.q: Which one of the following sequences is not convergent?
en.explanation:
$1+(-1)^n$ takes the values $0,2,0,2,\dots$: it oscillates and does not converge.
The other two converge to 1.
facts: A sequence with two subsequences tending to different limits diverges.

en.q: Every subgroup of an Abelian group is not
en.explanation: Every subgroup of an Abelian group is Abelian and normal ($gHg^{-1}=H$). But it need not be cyclic: the Klein four-group is a subgroup of itself, Abelian but not cyclic.
facts: In an Abelian group every subgroup is normal.

en.q: If $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+|\vec a\cdot\vec b|^2=144$ and $|\vec a|=4$, then $|\vec b|$ is equal to
en.explanation:
$|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2$ (Lagrange's identity).
$16|\vec b|^2=144\Rightarrow|\vec b|=3$.

en.q: If $\vec F=x^2y\,\hat i+xz\,\hat j+2yz\,\hat k$, then the value of $\mathrm{div}\,\mathrm{curl}\,\vec F$ is
en.explanation:

Here $\mathrm{curl}\,\vec F=(2z-x)\hat i+0\,\hat j+(z-x^2)\hat k$, whose divergence is $-1+0+1=0$.

en.q: If $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ are constant vectors, then $\nabla([\vec r,\vec a,\vec b])$ is equal to
en.explanation:
$[\vec r,\vec a,\vec b]=\vec r\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=\vec c\cdot\vec r$ with $\vec c=\vec a\times\vec b$ constant.
$\nabla(\vec c\cdot\vec r)=\vec c=\vec a\times\vec b$.
facts: $\nabla(\vec c\cdot\vec r)=\vec c$ for a constant vector $\vec c$.

en.q: The value of $(\vec c\times\vec a)\times(\vec a\times\vec b)$ is
en.explanation:
With $\vec u=\vec c\times\vec a$: $\vec u\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=(\vec u\cdot\vec b)\vec a-(\vec u\cdot\vec a)\vec b$.
$\vec u\cdot\vec a=0$ and $\vec u\cdot\vec b=[\vec c\,\vec a\,\vec b]=[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$. So the result is $[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]\,\vec a$.
notes: The vector is along $\vec a$, not $\vec b$.
The vector is along $\vec a$, not $\vec c$.
facts: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times(\vec a\times\vec c)=[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]\,\vec a$.

en.q: If $\vec A\times\vec B=\vec C\times\vec D$ and $\vec A\times\vec C=\vec B\times\vec D$, then vectors $\vec A-\vec D$ and $\vec B-\vec C$ are
en.explanation:
Subtract: $\vec A\times(\vec B-\vec C)=\vec C\times\vec D-\vec B\times\vec D=\vec D\times(\vec B-\vec C)$.
So $(\vec A-\vec D)\times(\vec B-\vec C)=\vec 0$: the vectors are parallel.
facts: $\vec u\times\vec v=\vec0$ with non-zero vectors means $\vec u\parallel\vec v$.

en.q: If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are non-coplanar unit vectors such that $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\dfrac{\vec b+\vec c}{\sqrt2}$, then the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ is
en.explanation:
$\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$. Since $\vec b,\vec c$ are independent, compare coefficients:
$\vec a\cdot\vec c=\frac1{\sqrt2}$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$. So the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ is $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.
notes: That is the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec c$.
facts: $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$.

en.q: If $\vec V_1,\vec V_2,\vec V_3$ are three non-zero vectors such that $\vec V_1\times\vec V_2=\vec V_3$, $\vec V_2\times\vec V_3=\vec V_1$, then
en.explanation:
The vectors are mutually perpendicular, so $|\vec V_3|=|\vec V_1||\vec V_2|$ and $|\vec V_1|=|\vec V_2||\vec V_3|$.
Then $|\vec V_3|=|\vec V_2|^2|\vec V_3|$, so $|\vec V_2|=1$ and $|\vec V_1|=|\vec V_3|$.
notes: In fact $\vec V_1\times\vec V_3=-|\vec V_1|^2\vec V_2$.
facts: For perpendicular vectors $|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec a||\vec b|$.

en.q: The equation $\left|\dfrac{z-3}{z+3}\right|=2$ represents
en.explanation: $|z-3|=2|z+3|$ gives $x^2+y^2+10x+9=0$: a circle with centre $(-5,0)$ and radius 4.
notes: A hyperbola needs a difference of distances.
An ellipse needs a sum of distances.
facts: $\left|\frac{z-a}{z-b}\right|=k\ne1$ is a circle; $k=1$ is a straight line.

en.q: If $x_n=\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2^n}\right)+i\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2^n}\right)$, $n\in\mathbb N$, then $\lim_{n\to\infty}(x_1x_2x_3\cdots x_n)$ is

en.q: If $f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y)$ for $z\ne0$, $f(0)=0$, where $u(x,y)=\dfrac{x^3-y^3}{x^2+y^2}$, $v(x,y)=\dfrac{x^3+y^3}{x^2+y^2}$, then the value of $\lim_{z\to0}\frac{f(z)-f(0)}{z-0}$, along $y=x$, will be
en.explanation:
On $y=x$: $u=0$, $v=\dfrac{2x^3}{2x^2}=x$, so $f(z)=ix$ and $z=x(1+i)$.
$\dfrac{f(z)}{z}=\dfrac{i}{1+i}=\dfrac{i(1-i)}{2}=\dfrac{1+i}{2}$.
notes: This is the limit along the real axis; the function is not differentiable at 0.
facts: Different limits along different paths show $f$ is not differentiable at 0, even though C–R hold there.

en.q: If $\omega\,(\ne1)$ is cube root of unity, then the value of $(1+\omega^2+2\omega)^{3n}-(1+\omega+2\omega^2)^{3n}$ is
en.explanation:
$1+\omega^2+2\omega=(1+\omega+\omega^2)+\omega=\omega$ and $1+\omega+2\omega^2=\omega^2$.
$\omega^{3n}-\omega^{6n}=1-1=0$.
